# Aggregate Validations {#sec-aggregate-validations}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

Every method in the previous chapter checked each row in turn. Aggregate validations check a column
as a whole. Instead of checking that each value is positive, they check that the column's total,
average, or standard deviation is where you expect it to be. The column is reduced to a single
number, and that number is the one and only test unit for the step.

Going from many test units to one changes how you read the result. A per-row check tells you how
many values failed, while an aggregate check can only tell you whether the summary value passed or
failed. That makes aggregate checks suited to a different kind of question, one about the column
overall rather than about individual entries. This chapter covers the three families (sums,
averages, and standard deviations), the `tol=` argument used for reconciliation, and what it means
in practice for a step to have exactly one test unit.

We use the `game_revenue` dataset throughout, mainly its `item_revenue` and `session_duration`
columns. For reference, the total of `item_revenue` is about 8,687, the mean of `session_duration`
is about 25.6, and the standard deviation of `item_revenue` is about 13.2.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
```

## When an aggregate is the right check

An aggregate check fits when the property you care about belongs to the column rather than to any
one row. The clearest case is reconciliation, where a total has to match a figure from somewhere
else, such as a revenue sum that must agree with an accounting ledger. No per-row check can express
this, because no single value is right or wrong on its own. Only the sum can be compared to the
expected figure.

Aggregates are also useful for plausibility monitoring, where you know roughly what an average or a
standard deviation should be and want to hear about it when that changes. If the average order
value suddenly halves, that often points to an upstream problem, even when no individual row looks
broken and every per-row check on the column still passes. Summary statistics are also cheap to
compute, so a few aggregate checks add very little to the cost of running a plan.

## Checking a column total

The `col_sum_gt()`, `col_sum_lt()`, `col_sum_ge()`, `col_sum_le()`, and `col_sum_eq()` methods
compare a column's sum against a value, with one method for each comparison operator. Here we check
that total revenue is above a minimum of 5,000.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_sum_gt(columns="item_revenue", value=5000)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The report shows a single test unit, and it passes because total revenue across the 2,000 rows is
about 8,687. A per-row check on the same column would have produced 2,000 test units, but the sum
reduces the column to one number, so the step passes or fails as a whole. If we flip the check and
require the total to be under 5,000, it fails.
